segments.text: My name is Jean-Marie Kananura. I'm the Chief Investment Officer at Kigali International Financial Center. It's an institution that is mandated by the government of Rwanda to develop, but also to position Rwanda as an international financial center.

So that, as you may know, traditionally, if investors, be it private or institutional investors, want to structure, let's say, an infrastructure fund, they will probably go to register that fund in Luxembourg or Singapore, right? So what we are putting in place really is, through KIFC, is to give an African alternative for capital for domiciliation. So it's my pleasure to be here today with these wonderful panelists. in case you want to blame someone for gender balance, I'm not the one who chose the speakers.

So I will invite the panelists to introduce themselves, starting with you, Jérôme, like one minute, maybe less, and then we can start the conversation. Good afternoon, everybody. It's a pleasure and an honor to be there, especially in this panel.

I'm the CEO of SATAREM America, which is both an engineering company based out of New York, but also a developer and investor in Africa into biofuels, meaning ethanol and sustainable aviation fuel. I would say, certain knowledge on how to structure finance regarding complicated projects in emerging markets. So I would be happy to give you our experience in this.
And I must say that financing SMRs and nuclear projects is really something which will be complicated, but definitely achievable. Thank you, Jérôme. Yes, over to you.
Thank you very much. My name is Dr. Hosea Kili from CPF Group Kenya. We are pension scheme administrators, one of the largest in Kenya.
A newly opened office here in Rwanda, Kigali. And we are in the business of investing pension funds in different sectors of the economy. Thank you.
Thank you. Hello, I am Denis Charles Kouassi, director of a pension fund management institution, which we call the Pension Funds Committee. We have a portfolio worth $3 billion.

We invest in companies, in the financial sector, in the energy sector. We also invest in compulsory jobs. And we are the first investor in the regional stock exchange, which is the stock of several African countries in West Africa.

My name is Meshack Bandawe, the secretary general of the Africa Social Security Association. This is the association of the pension funds and social security in Africa, which was established here in Rwanda in the year 2007, and was temporarily headquartered in Nairobi, Kenya, before permanently headquartered in Arusha, Tanzania. The intention is to work together, share experience, and to pursue the improvement of the social security sector in Africa, including the joint investment on the infrastructure project.

Good afternoon, everybody. I'm Erik Fernstrom. I'm the regional director in charge of infrastructure at the World Bank, covering Eastern and Southern Africa, which is about 23 of the countries in the subcontinent.
I cover energy issues as well as transport and urban development issues within the bank. And today I'm also somewhat representing our private sector colleagues at IFC. Thank you.
Good afternoon, everybody. My name is Kevin Kariuki. I'm the vice president for power, energy, climate change, and green growth at the African Development Bank.
I'm a power engineer through and through, starting with utility operations. I have been a researcher. I was involved in the unbundling of the U.K. power system.
I have been a developer for 20 years, and now I've been at the African Development Bank for six years. So if you cut my body, you'll see electrons flowing through and through. Thank you.

Thank you very much. Before we start, we set up this discussion really as a kind of room discussion. Our panelists are responding to this as if, let's say, a real project is on their desk, and you have to make a decision whether you have to invest or not.

So we'll be happy to understand what are the considerations, what you'll be looking at from your different perspective, but also what will be the risk and what will, let's say, make you run away from this project. I will start by my neighbor here, Jerome. From a developer perspective, every infrastructure deal begins with the project itself.

Before a financier evaluates return, they assess whether the project has been designed, structured, and is credible enough to dissolve capital. What are you looking at, and how are you advising your clients to structure this type of project? Thank you. and we will in the future, invest in a nuclear project, in Rwanda, for instance, the first thing we would look at would be the off-take contract and the off-taker.

We need a very credible off-taker, with all the guarantees that the lenders will require. I think this is really the first point. The second point would be to make sure that we present to the lenders a financial model that closes, and not something that creates losses for the next 20 years.
So these, I think, would be the first two items to present to lenders, I would say, as a preliminary project.

From a CPF perspective, as an investor, what is your diligence question that defines whether a nuclear infrastructure is investable, or what would make you, I'd say, run away from it? Yeah. I think for us, the capital allocators, on behalf of our members, the pension scheme members, as an institutional investor, one of the critical points, of course, is that this opportunity presents reliable and sustainable cash flows. That is very important for the length of the project.

Secondly, who is backing it? We have to look at the credibility of the promoter, the developer of such a big project, knowing that nuclear energy ostensibly is known to have risks, particularly if not properly designed and maintained. The other issue we look at is, is there a government or sovereign support fully, because in such an investment of that nature, the sovereign should be involved in a big way, and there should also be quite elaborate credit enhancement mechanisms by very strong credit guarantee institutions. The other one for us, long-term investors also, would be the issue of liquidity.

Is there, because we have to pay out our pensioners, so although it is a long-term investment, we expect it to have some elements of liquidity, whereby we could be able to draw out some of the resources. And finally, we would be looking at the political situation. A nuclear project, I could imagine, is a generational investment from one generation to another.

So the issue is, how is the political environment supporting such an investment, or is it one of those projects that may be rejected by a different generation of leadership, and therefore would be an issue. Finally, environmental concerns must be fully attended to and mitigated to make sure that we do not end up losing any of the funds we invest, because we have to assure our fiduciaries that their money is safe. Thank you.

Thank you very much. If I build on that, before I will stay with you, Hosea, could you maybe expand on the exit option also? Is it something that you're also looking at as an investor, and how would you basically assess it? Thank you. Yeah.

As I said, I think I did mention the issue of liquidity. Now, liquidity would be presented in several ways. One, of course, would be, is there a clawback mechanism by the developer of the investment in terms of uptake of any equity exited by us, if there is equity? And if it is a debt arrangement, is the instrument which has been used to raise capital, has it been listed and tradable in the capital market? That would be the areas of exit mechanism to enable venture funds to exit whenever they feel they need to move either to different investments or just to draw down for the purpose of paying members.
Thank you. Thank you very much. I'll come back to you, Jerome.

I think I have a second question for you around the risk that a developer realistically is expected to absorb or mitigate, whether construction schedule, technology performance, operations, or life cycle costs, and where does sovereign or DFI backing remain indispensable? That's a good question. So, yes, of course, as a developer, we need to mitigate all the risk. That means technical, technological risk, environmental risk, country risk.

But this is, I think, for us, part of the process of developing a project. What we think will be more complicated is the structure of financing, because my neighbor has been talking about cash flow and so on, but when you develop a project and you initiate a project, you are far from cash flowing. So the difficulty is on being able to raise the debt and to raise the equity on the project.

I must say for such a project, like an SMR, where the amount of a project cost could easily reach $1 billion, you need to have blended finance, and I think that has been said at several panels here, meaning bringing ECA, DFIs, and commercial banking. But I think the biggest challenge will be really the equity, because on a project like this, if we talk about IFC, for instance, we might ask for 50-50 gearing, meaning that you have to bring 50% of equity, and I think, as my neighbor also said before, it's important that there is a sovereign involvement. Once you have all this together, I think the project can really be a goal.
Okay, thank you very much. Building on that, I'm going to go to my friend Charles. Should I ask the question in French? You will answer in French, then the translation.

As you wish. The question I have for you is, as a social security institution, how do you analyze the risks? What are the important elements that would make you invest in a nuclear project of this nature? As a pension fund, we have three criteria for profitability. First, financial profitability, because you receive money today from a worker, and you develop it in 20 or 30 years.

So, when they pay you 1,000 francs in fees today, in 30 years, it will turn into 15,000 to cancel inflation. So, that's what we call financial profitability. Then there is economic profitability, because we are a social security institution, and we are powered by corporate fees.

So, if the economy is doing well, the companies will hire, and we will receive more contributions. And the third criterion is the social one, that is, as a social security institution, we have to think of the weakest, the most vulnerable people. And so, when we produce enough wealth, we have the opportunity to take care of these vulnerable people with more favorable conditions.

But I think that, beyond these criteria, the most important role that pension funds will play is first of all the long-term resource. Because, you see, today, we have a reserve of six years of payment of benefits. So, that means that we can afford to mobilize funds over decades.

This is very important. The liquidity aspect is solved by making sure that a good part, at least 30 to 40 percent, of our deposits are liquid deposits, in the short and medium term. But 70 percent of the deposits can be made over much longer periods.
And I would also like to add that we are already in the energy sector. We are an investor in the energy sector. In a Pan-African group called Eranove, we have 15 percent of this group.

And we are also shareholders in the operational institution that manages energy in this group. And we co-invest with investment funds, with the state of Ivory Coast. And I came here to see if there are any interesting projects that I can invest in to make money.

I have no doubt that we have to go to the nuclear sector. So, I don't need to be convinced that we have to go to the nuclear sector. I came to see what the projects in the nuclear sector so that we can play our role in this process.
Thank you very much. I'm going to your neighbor, Meshach. I know that most pension funds are not looking at nuclear as an asset class.
At least not yet. Is it something that you are eventually looking at? And if yes, when can we expect the African pension fund coming in to support these very important initiatives to begin with.
Thank you.

Just to complement with our nuclear initiatives, the pension funds in Africa are in the process of establishing an infrastructure fund for Africa. Just the intention of working together to invest in essential projects including the transportation, roads, railways, ports, airports, energy, digital telecom, agriculture, industrialization. We have decided to establish an infrastructure fund.

When this is done, it will be operated by a very reputable fund manager under the supervision of the CEO and trustees of the fund. Why are we doing that? The pension funds have massive assets under management. We think that part of it can be allocated to the infrastructure.

According to recent records, the pension funds are over $800 billion in social security institutions in Africa. Which part of it can be invested in infrastructure and ensure sustainability of the pension funds and reliable cash flow to meet our long-term obligations. We do this because of the diversification opportunity to share risk and resource in implementing the infrastructure projects because currently the investment is on the short-term.

We are thinking on the other side of the coin to invest in long-term investments. But also aligned with the social agenda and other programs around the continent. I think we have a big role to play in the economic development in African countries which at the end have the multiplier effect on the pension funds, creating jobs, improving GDP, managing the poverty level and improving the quality of life of the people in Africa.

In terms of the progress made, so far we have collaborated with the African Development Bank, AFDB, the support of Dr. Sidi and also the AFC and TDB. They are collaborating with the pension funds to finalize the investment policy statement and other legal documents for the establishment of the fund. We expect the policy statement will be done by the end of this May to be circulated to the member countries for approval in their respective authorities.

When it's done, we expect the fund to be launched in Abidjan during the first summit which will be hosted by CNPS in July this year. This is an opportunity, nuclear energy is an investment opportunity for the pension funds to pursue and we recommend we need to work together between the nuclear initiatives and the pension funds to make sure this is going to happen. Thank you very much.

This is great news and I hope that the fund will be domiciled on the continent. This leads to Eric, I think the World Bank has already decided that nuclear is an asset class that you can now invest in. From your perspective, what are the real preconditions for bankability before guarantee? Debt instruments or technical assistance that can crowd in private institutional capital? Thank you.

First of all, the first smell test that we do for any power project that we support comes from the public good side. Does the project make sense from a ratepayer perspective? Is the project aligned or below marginal cost of power in the country? Is it competitive? Does it offer advantages that we want to see in a country like Rwanda, for instance, in terms of growth, job creation and general wealth creation in the country? For that, it needs to be competitive. If it is not, and if it is a new technology, the question then comes into whether there are ways to get below that bar through clever structuring of grants, technology support, blended finance between public and private and a broad partnership around it.

This is probably where we end up in the initial programs in Africa on nuclear power because the technology is not necessarily available everywhere and at the production scale that it will beat every single competitor on its own. I think that we need to be very agnostic in terms of how we structure these financing structures between public and private and how we bring in partners that can actually alleviate that. I think that only when we have a program that actually makes sense at that level, we can go into things like structuring, guarantees, risk mitigation for investors, gearing ratios, as well as compliance, which obviously will be a major issue around nuclear growth from a safety perspective as well as more of a traditional ESG lens.

But that comes later. The second question is in terms of risk management, which layers of risk are best handled through government policy reform? Which one is handled through institutions like yours? And which one should remain with a private investor? That's a big question. But I think I touched upon it yesterday.

I think the aspects of nuclear safety, the aspects of regulatory predictability and compliance obviously rest with the government and the sovereign to a large extent. If the country doesn't have those frameworks, it is not investable. What remains? The residual risk.

I think there is a careful calibration between the commercial risk the investor takes, the risk that lenders take, which tends to be a lot less, and what we can offset. I think the World Bank, there is a perception that we can absorb a lot of risk. Actually, what we do is we describe it as a halo effect.

We have a partnership with the government. We see further into the decision and the commitment of the government on policy reform. And we are able to put our name behind the government's commitment to offset some of that risk.

But it rests on the commitment of the government at the end of the day. If we say we will provide a liquidity guarantee for an off-taker to pay his bills, it's based on a belief that the government and that off-taker utility, for instance, actually is on the right path and will make good on those commitments. In a way, it's a country risk, however you bundle it with MDB guarantees, etc.
Thank you very much. This is great. Over to you.

Kevin, from an FDB perspective, what would a credible African nuclear capital look like? I think the way to address that question is to contextualize the fact that, to date, most of the nuclear power plants have been developed through the public sector. There are decent examples and there are good reasons for that. The one thing that is obvious and everybody will tell you is that the time overruns for nuclear power plants is significant.

I read earlier this week that some plants in Finland and France that are due for commissioning are a decade late. The 50% cost overruns is not unusual. I would expect that there would be significant sovereign debt and also significant sovereign equity.

I'll give you the example of Seawell in the UK. The government of the UK is taking 45% equity interest in the project. The sovereign wealth fund of the UK is paying an entire 100% of the debt but trying to unsell some of that debt.

They've already sold about 15%. In terms of debt and equity, I would expect that you'll have about 20% to 40% equity and about 60% to 80% to be debt. However, in a project, maybe in Africa, what you could also do is to try and mobilize concessional funding that can be on lend to the investor or the project company to be able to also reduce the cost of the tariffs eventually.

I think at the end of the day, it's nothing new. It has to be debt and equity. The thing is, where does that debt come from and where does that equity come from? I must say that to date, based on what we have, in order to ensure, for example, if there's that long a delay, it's unlikely that the private sector will meet the additional costs that are associated with the delay.
Hence, you need significant sovereign debt and equity in the project. Let me stop there. Thank you very much.

You spoke about the portion of equity and debt. What about the portion of stock that must be catalytic before the commercial capital comes in? I think before the commercial capital comes in, I know it's always easy to look at DFI, but even us as DFIs, and Eric will tell you, we need to repay this money. We need significant certainty on the technology and the timelines for the project.

It is possible that you could be able to get some little multilateral financing, but to date, there is not significant multilateral financing that comes from MDBs. However, it is possible that you could be able to get something catalytic, just like when we had wind technology coming in, we had a lot of climate financing that came to help us to overcome the initial technological risks. It is possible that the fact that the taxonomy today recognizes nuclear as a clean source of energy, there is a possibility that in view of what is happening geopolitically, there could be a need to promote nuclear technology and therefore facilitate availability of concessionary funding that would be catalytic, as you call it.
Thank you. I'm looking at the time that we still have. I just want to thank our panelists.

We have another discussion that we want to have. We want to move to a more practical discussion, but also we want to invite two experts on the panel to reflect on what was gathered from the mentee and for the QR code questions, as well as some reflection from what we discussed here on the panel. I just want to thank my dear panelists here.
